title: Infant respiratory syncytial virus and childhood asthma: a nationwide phenotyping, sibling-controlled, and genome-wide association study

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines whether early-life respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection causes childhood recurrent wheeze or asthma (RW/A), focusing on causality, shared genetic liability, and distinct phenotypic trajectories in Finnish and Nordic populations.

analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: RSV-associated RW/A demonstrates higher inhaled medication use at ages 1–2 years but lower use after age 4, with lower mean blood eosinophils (0.34 vs 0.39×109/L; p=0.003) compared to RW/A without RSV hospitalization. analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not resolve whether shared genetic or environmental factors fully explain the RSV-asthma association, as unaffected siblings also showed elevated RW/A prevalence. analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review prioritizes long-term outcome monitoring in RSV prevention trials and suggests that distinct medication and eosinophil trajectories in RSV-associated RW/A may inform targeted surveillance strategies.

The findings emphasize the need for long-term monitoring in RSV prevention trials and targeted surveillance based on phenotypic differences.

title: Demographic and Clinical Determinants of Acute Bronchiolitis Outcomes in a Tertiary Pediatric Hospital in Dubai, United Arab Emirates

analysis.methods: Variables extracted included age, sex, nationality, gestational age, feeding type, family history of atopy, viral PCR results, initial oxygen saturation, and therapies received. analysis.summary_en: This retrospective study from a tertiary pediatric hospital in Dubai examined determinants of bronchiolitis outcomes in 232 infants aged 1–24 months admitted between October 2022 and March 2023. No demographic or clinical factors significantly influenced PICU admission or oxygen requirement, though a family history of atopy was associated with shorter hospital stays. Steroid use correlated with greater oxygen support but did not improve outcomes.
